claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to assess whether a system has a ferromagnetic ground state.
A lower computed total energy for a spin-polarized ferromagnetic configuration than for an appropriate competing magnetic configuration indicates a ferromagnetic ground state within the calculation.
A nonmagnetic configuration and a paramagnetic configuration can be treated as interchangeable comparison states for this test.
Transition-metal alloys with partially filled d bands may support localized magnetic moments.
The proposed method compares spin-polarized and non-spin-polarized DFT calculations at 0 K and zero external magnetic field.
Noncollinear magnetic calculations may be needed for some candidate systems.
The crystal lattice and electronic band structure permit unpaired electrons to interact through exchange coupling.
Exchange interactions can lower the total energy when spins align ferromagnetically.
Spin-polarized DFT captures magnetic exchange effects by allowing spin-dependent splitting of electronic energy levels.
A ferromagnetic state is preferred when its exchange-related energy gain exceeds competing energetic effects.
The candidate system will exhibit a noticeably lower total energy in the ferromagnetic configuration.
The candidate system will exhibit a finite magnetic moment per atom in the ferromagnetic calculation.
Non-spin-polarized DFT does not represent exchange-split energy levels.
Strongly correlated systems may require DFT+U or other many-body corrections.
The predicted magnetic energy difference is sensitive to the exchange-correlation functional.
The computed energy difference may vary with computational parameters.
Convergence with respect to k-point sampling and basis-set completeness should be checked.
Failure to obtain an energy lowering beyond computational error margins, or failure to obtain a finite magnetic moment, would falsify the stated prediction.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis is conditional—DFT indicates ferromagnetism only if the ferromagnetic state is lower in energy—whereas the predicted outcome states that the unspecified candidate system will show lower energy and a finite moment despite acknowledged system and parameter dependence.
